# Dual Implementation as Cross-Check

Build the same thing twice, in two different stacks, and keep both. The second implementation is not
redundancy — it is the only check available when there are no tests, because two independent
implementations agreeing is evidence and one implementation asserting is not.

## The strongest instance: lab 6

`lab6_Neo4j/viewer/pawlak.js` reimplements every [[cypher]] query as, in the repo's words, "the exact
analogue" in plain JavaScript, and renders the graph pictures and tables **beside the Cypher that
produces them**:

> "**Data note.** The dataset holds **39** countries; earlier drafts of the guide said 38 (and 950
> `HAS_VALUE`). The numbers were corrected to **39 objects / 975 edges** throughout — the import
> logic itself was already correct (it `MERGE`s one object per row)."
> — Discrete-Mathematics-Laboratories/lab6_Neo4j/README.md, 2026-07-10

That correction is the pattern paying out: a discrepancy between what the documentation claimed and
what a run produced was findable *because* the same system existed twice. See
[[pawlak-information-system]] and [[idempotent-loading]].

## The other instances

- **Lab 4, Python and browser.** Ackermann, Stirling and Nim exist as [[matplotlib]]/[[tkinter]]
  programs in `part1` and again as a zero-build JS app in `part2`.
- **Lab 02, two shapes of the same answer.** Eight questions answered both as `weblog` subcommands
  and as a single script — [[python-programming-laboratories]].
- **Lab 04, the teaching class beside the production one.**

> "`weblog.LogEntry` is the version the rest of the repository uses; the classes here are the teaching
> version, kept because writing the special methods by hand is the exercise."
> — Python-Programming-Laboratories/labs/04_classes/README.md, 2026-07-25

Recorded as a decision on [[keep-the-teaching-version]].

## When it is worth it, and when it is not

It works here because the systems are small and the second implementation costs hours, not weeks, and
because the *purpose* of the duplication is stated in the tree. It is closely related to
[[multiple-solutions-side-by-side]] — that pattern compares algorithms within one program; this one
compares whole implementations across stacks.

The cost is real and shows up in this repo: two copies drift. `guide.txt` still says "object count =
38" after the README says the correction was applied "throughout" — [[documentation-drift]]. Two
implementations cross-check each other only while someone is actually running both.
